 Mohsin Naqvi faces fresh questions as PCB's reported $25,000 NOC fee row hits Nepal league 
 Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) chief Mohsin Naqvi has found himself in another controversy as he faces fresh questions over the board's handling of no-objection certificates (NOCs) for Nepal Premier League (NPL). According to ESPNcricinfo, sources associated with the NPL said the PCB had put even previously issued NOCs on hold and sought around USD 25,000 for each Pakistani player.
 However, the report said it could not confirm whether the demand had been formally communicated to the league in writing. The report also added that PCB has not responded to ESPNcricinfo's request for comment.
 The development follows a similar controversy involving Major League Cricket (MLC) in the United States. In a July 17 report, PTI said the PCB had introduced a USD 25,000 fee for players' NOCs, leaving fast bowler Haris Rauf as Pakistan's sole representative in that season's MLC. Citing a franchise source, the report said Naqvi had reportedly defended the charge as the board's right and a source of revenue.
 The latest controversy also puts the spotlight on Naqvi's position as president of the Asian Cricket Council (ACC), which oversees cricket across the continent, including associate-member nations such as Nepal. The reported demand raises questions about the impact of the PCB's NOC policy on smaller cricket markets seeking to attract established Pakistani players.

 Naqvi has previously been at the centre of a high-profile cricket administration controversy. After India defeated Pakistan in the 2025 Asia Cup final, the Indian team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi, who was serving as ACC president. The presentation ended without India receiving the trophy. India captain Suryakumar Yadav later said he had seen officials leave with the silverware, describing the incident with the words, “Trophy leke bhaag gaye woh.”
 With the NPL issue, the key question is whether the reported fee was formally demanded and whether it is responsible for the hold on players' clearances. For now, the allegations remain attributed to reports and sources, rather than a publicly confirmed PCB directive.
